newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany finds first suspected victim of new CJD.
newsitem.headline: Germany finds first suspected victim of new CJD.

text.p: A 41-year-old woman who was buried on Saturday is believed to be a victim of a new form of the brain-wasting Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), the north German state of Schleswig-Holstein said.
Public concern about CJD has been growing since British scientists disclosed last March a probable link between mad cow disease, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), and CJD.

"If it is confirmed that it is Creutzfeld Jakob then it is the new version of the disease," a spokeswoman for the Schleswig-Holstein health ministry told Reuters in a reference to the short duration of the woman's illness.
It would be the first recorded death in Germany of the new form of CJD.

Twelve people in Britain are known to have died from the slowly incubated disease which is believed to result from eating BSE-infected beef. Three other cases have been diagnosed, one of them in France.
The new and quicker-acting form of CJD was identified last March. The older version is extremely rare.
The European Union imposed a ban on British beef after the British scientific research was made public last year. Britain has recorded the most BSE cases -- around 165,000 in the last 10 years.
The Schleswig-Holstein health ministry spokeswoman said that, if necessary, a post-mortem would be ordered on the woman's remains.

"We are taking the case very seriously...the important thing in this case is the age of the woman. We have never had a case of CJD in this state in somebody so young," she added. The old strain of CJD was usually only found in the elderly, she said.
The news of the death came as Germany's agriculture ministry sought to establish the origin of a cow which could be the first born in Germany to die of BSE.

When the case came to light earlier this week, the agriculture ministry announced the slaughter of more than 5,000 cattle imported from Britain and Switzerland. But on Friday the Agriculture Ministry said it was investigating the possibility that the calf had been imported illegally from Britain.

On Saturday, however, the ministry said the cow had no official registered ear tag, just one showing the animal's herd, prompting Spiegel magazine to say the cow must indeed have been born in Germany.
The ministry said it would not make a final pronouncement about the origin of the animal until all the uncertainty had been cleared up and genetic tests were performed on the cow.
The issue of the origin of the cow has stirred up controversy because if the cow was born in Germany to a British cow, it would add weight to fears that BSE can be transferred from mother to calf.
If experts prove this to be the case, 14,000 offspring of British and Swiss cows currently under observation in Germany could also be slaughtered.
